newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Special forces ring Seoul church, pressure unions.
newsitem.headline: Special forces ring Seoul church, pressure unions.

text.p: South Korean police on Friday tightened a security noose around a Seoul cathedral where a top strike leader was hiding from arrest, and the ruling camp scorned a dramatic offer by the fugitive for a televised debate.
Special force officers trained in unarmed combat guarded approaches to Myongdong cathedral, while police checked cars approaching the building.
The so-called "grabbers" -- hardened by years of street fighting -- are deployed during riots to rush into crowds and make arrests.
South Korea's Roman Catholic cardinal appealed to President Kim Young-sam during a meeting to "resolve the current situation with dialogue", a presidential spokesman said.

Strike leader Kwon Young-kil, president of the outlawed Korean Confederation of Trade Unions, challenged the chairman of the New Korean Party to a public debate over the new labour law that has sparked more than three weeks of stoppages.
He was taking up a suggestion by Lee for a televised, round-table discussion between New Korea Party leaders and unspecified union heads.
Kwon called on party chairman Lee Hong-koo to personally square off with him on camera. He also said the government must guarantee his safety from arrest.
The New Korea Party spurned the offer on the grounds that Kwon was a fugitive, and called on unions to put forward more suitable candidates.
"Even for a television debate, the law should be observed," a New Korea Party statement said. "There cannot be guarantees of safety for people who have legal problems."
Kwon and six deputies were all evading arrest in a ramshackle tent on the grounds of Myongdong, directing industrial action with portable telephones.
But the strikes have wound down and there were now just pockets of worker resistance.

The labour ministry said strikes were tapering off, with only 57,320 workers at 48 companies involved. The confederation put the figure at up to 200,000 and vowed to continue partial strikes in public services and manufacturing.
Seoul stocks fell 1.5 percent to 701.18 in afternoon trading on profit-taking after rallying for two straight days on relief that the strikes were fizzling.
Kwon had insisted that a debate did not imply his union was seeking dialogue over the law, which allows companies to lay off workers, replace strikers and extend work hours.
Wrangling over the debate indicated both sides were jockeying for position in a battle for public opinion.

Public support for the government was wavering, with many commentators comparing President Kim Young-sam to past strongman rulers for the way legislation that transforms South Korea's industrial landscape was rammed through parliament.
The law was passed in a dawn sitting of parliament on December 26 while opposition deputies slept.
A tough and inflexible posture on the bill has cost the government sympathy at home and triggered opposition by world labour organisations.

In what is widely viewed as an ominous warning of a crackdown, authorities have linked labour strife to North Korea and produced communist propaganda from Pyongyang they say is circulating among strikers.
The two Koreas have been technically at war since their 1950-53 conflict ended in a truce.

International labour organisations maintain the new law curbs worker rights to freedom of association by allowing the Federation of Korean Trade Unions to retain its monopoly on union representation until 2000.
Ten leaders of trade union organisations from around the world are to due to arrive next week to replace four others who were hustled out on Thursday.
South Korea's immigration chief said the 10 would be allowed in, but warned they would be deported if they took part in strike-related protests.
